# The Learning Path: the SupChains Way in 13 Emails

Everyone who downloads the SupChains Way folder (or subscribes at [supchains.com/newsletter](https://supchains.com/newsletter/?utm_source=chatgpt&utm_medium=plugin&utm_campaign=supchains-way)) receives a learning path of 13 emails written by Nicolas. The first three deliver four free chapters of *Demand Forecasting Best Practices*: chapters 1–2 (the five-step framework for demand planning excellence, and why we forecast demand, not sales), chapter 8 (forecasting metrics — "MAPE is the worst forecasting metric. Don't use it."), and chapter 12 (Forecast Value Added — "the cornerstone of demand planning excellence"; Nicolas doubts a supply chain can call itself good at demand planning unless it measures and delivers on FVA). The next ten are short lessons on the demand planning process. They say the same things as the articles, in fewer words; the summaries below keep the formulations practitioners tend to remember, so that an agent can quote them.

|---|---|---|
| 1 | Demand forecast vs. sales forecast vs. budget | A demand forecast is information for supply planners — not a sales target, a revenue target, or a budget |
| 2 | The sales team can't do it (alone) | Ask salespeople for insights, never for numbers |

## Lesson 1 — Demand forecast vs. sales forecast vs. budget

Many demand planning teams try their best to enrich their forecasts and fail to add real value — supply chain leaders usually get in touch after trying outlier cleaning, product segmentation, and ABC-XYZ, approaches Nicolas does not recommend. The root cause is most often external pressure to modify forecasts: finance wants the forecast to stick to the budget, sales wants it inflated to secure supply and stock. As long as leaders blur the lines between demand forecasting, sales targets, supply planning, and budget, they cannot expect accurate, unbiased forecasts from their teams. A demand forecast is a piece of information that supply planners use to make the right decisions — nothing more, nothing less. Sales forecasts are computed mechanically from supply-unconstrained demand forecasts and supply plans; during shortages, the demand forecast can be much higher than the sales forecast, and that is normal. **A demand forecast is not a sales target, a revenue target, or a budget** — colleagues who don't understand the difference can't deliver good forecasts.

## Lesson 2 — The sales team can't do it (alone)

A common red flag of low supply chain maturity: the sales team takes over demand forecasting, either generating the baseline or getting the final say on the planners' numbers. Salespeople are incentivized to exceed sales targets, so they inflate forecasts to secure stock, or lower them to set easier goals — biased, inaccurate forecasts from a labor-intensive process that also takes salespeople away from what they do best: selling. To scale the process on unbiased forecasts, three steps: (1) collect and clean order and master data for the engine, and feed it the promotional calendar and historical shortages — which "nearly no one does"; (2) let the engine generate the baseline automatically; (3) let demand planners enrich it with insights the model doesn't have. When reviewing forecasts with salespeople, **don't ask for a baseline or expected sales figures — ask for insights**: do they know anything the model doesn't, such as a client going through a difficult time who will soon reduce its orders? Even then, people may share only the information that supports their own agenda.

## Lesson 3 — Don't forecast sales, or else

The core concept: **forecast supply-unconstrained demand, not supply-constrained sales** — what clients want, not what you plan to sell. Constrained sales forecasts pilot supply orders into a vicious circle: shortages lead to zero forecasts, zero forecasts to zero supply orders, and the shortage never ends. Unconstrained demand forecasts let you buy the right amounts even during shortages. (If you really want sales and revenue forecasts, infer them mechanically by matching the demand forecast against the supply plan.) If you don't exclude shortages from historical orders, you are forecasting sales: the engine reads shortages as low-demand periods, and planners then have to second-guess the forecasts — or worse, "correct" historical demand, which Nicolas calls arguably the worst possible demand planning practice. Shortages also skew accuracy KPIs: measure accuracy during shortages and you are paying planners to predict shortages and set forecasts to zero — which produces more shortages. "You are paying your team to deteriorate your forecasts." A team spending its time predicting shortages is a serious sign something is wrong. The three steps: **flag shortages using historical inventory data; never measure forecasting accuracy during a shortage; make sure the engine bypasses shortages** rather than treating them as low demand. Without them you stay stuck with sales forecasting, and supply planners end up manually overriding constrained forecasts.

## Lesson 4 — You need to beat this benchmark

Asked how they know their team does a good job, practitioners answer "we want to be more accurate than last month," "better than last year," or "we try to beat our target" — a closed loop, since nobody knows how to set the target. None of these works: this month's accuracy depends mostly on this month's inherent forecastability — a product launch or a massive promotion makes forecasts less accurate through no fault of the planners. Industry benchmarks don't work either: expensive, rarely matching your KPIs, granularity, and horizon, and comparing businesses with different portfolios, clients, and promotions — some companies are more accurate than others within the same industry, legitimately. **Compare yourself to a moving average**: it is free and straightforward, and it forecasts better or worse exactly when a market or period is easier or harder to forecast. If your team beats it, it adds value — it improves on what the data already says, rather than repeating it. Per twenty years of academic analysis, planners have only about a 50% chance of improving a forecast; the following lessons are about raising that likelihood.

## Lesson 5 — Five questions to reboot the process

When forecasts stay biased and inaccurate despite every effort, outlier cleaning and product segmentation won't rescue the process — and when maturity is low, salespeople will bend the final numbers to their agenda. Reboot how planners look at forecasts by asking them to focus **only** on five questions:

1. Have we won new markets or new clients?
2. Have we lost markets or clients?
3. Are we launching new products?
4. Are we discontinuing products?
5. Are there any product transitions?

The five questions shield the forecast from sales and finance agendas, and make sure planners spend review time only where they have new information to add.

## Lesson 6 — Three things planners should not do

Product segmentation, zero-touch forecasts, outlier detection: ideas that push planners to work harder without delivering much added value, if any. Demand planning should be efficient and focused. Three practices Nicolas always advises clients to drop:

- **Don't waste time reviewing outliers.** Consultants and software vendors bill their time for statistical outlier detection, and some planners spend theirs adjusting historical sales; the added value is thin at best. In VN1, not a single winning team performed outlier detection, and SupChains needed statistical outlier detection on one single project in five years. Invest that time in **data cleaning at the transactional level** instead — "if you are not cleaning data at the transactional level, you're doing it wrong" — and use a robust engine that copes with shortages, promotions, and the other business drivers. Then outlier detection isn't needed anymore.
- **Don't review or tweak forecasting models.** The automated optimization at the core of the engine should be, well, automated: reasonable forecasts without planner involvement. If humans can systematically beat the engine without information the model lacks, the engine needs improving. Don't waste planners' brains on selecting models: fix the engine, and use humans for added-value tasks.
- **Don't worry about current or future inventory levels.** That is not demand forecasting. Forecasting demand is about what clients will want to buy, not how much you will sell: sales are constrained by supply; demand is not. Supply planners own inventory and safety stocks; demand planners estimate future client demand, unbiased.

## Lesson 7 — Three things planners should always do

Demand planners should see themselves as **journalists and reporters**, not as accountants reviewing time series and manually tweaking models. The forecasting game is about gaining more insights, data, and information about your markets:

1. **Collect and clean data** — the most important activity: master data, product transitions, the promotional calendar, and the order book must be consistent and well maintained. Planners are *data stewards*.
2. **Gather extra insights** beyond the structured data fed to the engine — planners should know more about future demand than what is already in the tool: contact clients, read the marketing plan, anticipate price changes. Planners are *investigators*.
3. **Enrich baseline forecasts** — *if you know something, do something*. Once a planner learns something the engine doesn't know, it's time to enrich the forecast and make it better. Planners are *forecast augmenters*.

## Lesson 8 — How does your process compare?

"How does our accuracy compare to our industry?" really means "is our demand planning process effective?" Industry benchmarks can't answer it: they are expensive, built on poorly recorded data and inconsistent KPIs, and they compare companies in different markets selling different portfolios — a competitor in mature markets with a narrow range will naturally be more accurate than one in newer markets with a much wider range. Comparing against last year, last month, last quarter, or other markets doesn't work either: some months are naturally easier (seasonality, promotions, competitor activity) and some years go more smoothly than others — think of 2020; January 2024 versus January 2023 is apples and oranges. **Compare yourself to a moving average, and aim to reduce its error by 10 to 30%.** Unlike industry benchmarks, moving averages are free, simple, and fair, and they provide a dynamic benchmark that moves with market conditions. "Surely we beat it — it's in our forecasting software package?" Many don't: a moving average being available as a baseline model guarantees nothing about your baseline forecast or your process. Try the comparison; you'll be surprised. And don't track accuracy alone — bias is essential.

## Lesson 9 — Incentivizing planners won't make your forecasts more accurate

In all his years helping supply chain leaders optimize their forecasts, Nicolas has never heard "we increased our planners' bonuses, and it massively improved our accuracy." Incentivizing planners on accuracy thresholds is unfair: they work on stable or unstable markets and segments whose accuracy is naturally high or low, with no agency over it. If anything, incentivize Forecast Value Added — how much value planners add to the process — but incentives are a double-edged sword: they may motivate the extra mile, or push people toward shortcuts that maximize FVA without tangible value, such as convoluted metrics with exceptions or comparisons against weak benchmarks. **Don't incentivize accuracy. Incentivize FVA only once it is properly set up and understood.**

## Lesson 10 — The three keys to successful demand planning

Excellent demand planning relies on three key steps:

1. **Track Forecast Value Added.** In every training and lecture, Nicolas pauses on the FVA slide: it is *the* most important part of the training, the one nobody can do without.
2. **Use automated, bulletproof machine learning.** Supply chains forecast hundreds of thousands of data points every week or month; they can't do it by paying humans to generate baselines. *Automated* means planners don't worry about model selection or parameter fine-tuning — a scalable process with as little human intervention as possible. *Bulletproof* means the engine copes with all your usual business drivers. On every project, Nicolas feeds three things to the model when available: **historical shortages, promotions, and the future order book** — they make forecasts much more accurate.
3. **Insight-driven enrichment.** *If you know something, do something* should be every demand planner's motto: change a forecast only when you know something the baseline model doesn't. Insight-driven reviews focus planners on the product-market combinations where they are most likely to add value. Many consultants and software vendors advise product segmentation instead — reviewing high-revenue, high-variability products — but high variability doesn't mean humans have a better chance than computers at producing good forecasts. **Don't segment your products. Stick to insight-driven reviews: what do you know?**
